newsitem.title: USA: Judge sets Nov. 18 court date for Katzenberg suit.
newsitem.headline: Judge sets Nov. 18 court date for Katzenberg suit.

text.p: A California judge Wednesday set a Nov. 18 trial date for former Walt Disney Co. studio chief Jeffrey Katzenberg's $250 million breach-of-contract suit against the company.
At a hearing here, Los Angeles Superior Court Judge John Ouderkirk scheduled a status conference for Nov. 13 and a trial date of Nov. 18.

Katzenberg, who left Disney in 1994 after Chairman Michael Eisner decided not to promote him to president, is seeking $250 million from his former employer, based on his claim that he should be entitled to a portion of the studio's profits from blockbusters such as "Beauty and the Beast" and "The Lion King".
Disney has repeatedly denied Katzenberg's claim, saying he relinquished his rights to share in the profits of those films when he opted out of his contract early.
Hollywood insiders say a lawsuit involving Disney and Katzenberg could prove damaging to both sides as details of what has been a private squabble between two Hollywood giants become public.
Last August, there was an effort to settle the dispute privately but it quickly broke down after both sides failed to reach an agreement.
Katzenberg's attorney, Bert Fields, said the former studio chief is looking foward to resolving the matter in court.
"We think we're right about the case and we want to get it in front of a jury to decide it," Fields told reporters outside the court room.
A spokesman for the Burbank, Calif.-based entertainment giant said the company was preparing for trial.
"Now that a trial date has been set, the facts will be made public in a court of law rather than spin doctor lawyers," Disney spokesman John Dreyer said.

The dispute between Katzenberg and his former mentor Eisner has captivated many in Hollywood, largely because both men are strong-willed executives who once were good friends and now rarely speak to each other.

When Eisner and Katzenberg took over at Disney in 1984, the studio was in last place. Four years later, the studio was back on track, reflecting solid results from Disney's animation department under Katzenberg's supervision.

The relationship began to sour, however, in 1994 following the death of Disney President Frank Wells. After being passed over for Wells' job Katzenberg exercised an early-out clause in his contract and passed up some $100 million in stock options.
A few months later Katzenberg founded a new studio called DreamWorks SKG with music mogul David Geffen and director Steven Spielberg.
